title: Inverse_mass = 0: a pinned anchor ignores gravity while a test body falls
abstract: inverse_mass = 0: a pinned anchor ignores gravity while a test body falls — dynamic notebook
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `obj0` | `point` | `mass = 5`, `position = [0, 10, 0]`, `velocity = [0, 0, 0]` |
| `obj1` | `point` | `mass = 1`, `position = [1, 10, 0]`, `velocity = [0, 0, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`point`** — a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia. `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`velocity`** — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is OFF** (`g_constant = 0`). The simulator's default is 1, so this had to be said explicitly; without it, bodies that are supposed only to bounce or to be held by joints would also attract each other.
- **Uniform gravity** is `[0, -9.81, 0]` metres per second squared, applied to every body alike.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
eom:
There are 2 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = m_i g

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `m_i g` — the uniform field, here `g = [0, -9.81, 0]`
constraints:
**This model has no joints.** Nothing algebraic relates the coordinates, so the system is an ordinary differential equation rather than a differential-algebraic one, and it needs no Lagrange multipliers and no constraint Jacobian.

That does not mean nothing is conserved. Energy, linear momentum and angular momentum are still exact consequences of the equations of motion, and comparing them before and after a run is the honest way to judge the integration.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 2 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
2 bodies x 13 numbers = 26 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

There are no algebraic constraints, so the whole of the mechanics above is one first-order system

```
dy/dt = f(t, y),   y in R^26
```

handed to the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

The right-hand side `f` unpacks `y` into bodies, computes every force and torque, and packs the derivatives back in the same 13-per-body order.

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`new point` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia**, left unnamed, so it takes the next automatic name `objN`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 5` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `position = [0, 10, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `velocity = [0, 0, 0]` — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.

---

`set obj0.inverse_mass = 0` changes one property of the body `obj0` after creation. `inverse_mass` is one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.


Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `position = [1, 10, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.

steps.code:
sim.do("new point { mass = 5, position = [0, 10, 0], velocity = [0, 0, 0] }")
sim.do("set obj0.inverse_mass = 0")
sim.do("new point { mass = 1, position = [1, 10, 0], velocity = [0, 0, 0] }")

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.g_constant = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -9.81, 0]` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `uniform_gravity` is a uniform gravitational field applied to every body, as `[gx, gy, gz]` in metres per second squared. This is the everyday 'g' of falling, entirely separate from the mutual attraction above.

The value expected here is `[0, -9.81, 0]`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

steps.title: Measure (2)
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 4 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`list` prints every body with its name, shape, mass and current state, tagging static bodies and walls. It takes no arguments.

---

`energy` prints the total kinetic plus potential energy of the whole system. Take it before and after a run: for a closed system with no dissipation the two should agree to near machine precision, and how well they agree is the honest measure of the integration. It takes no arguments.

---

`momentum` prints the total linear momentum, summed over every body. With no external force it is exactly conserved, and it is conserved through collisions too, because every impulse is applied equal and opposite to the pair. It takes no arguments.

---

`angmom` prints the total angular momentum about the origin, including both the spin of each body and the orbital contribution of its motion about the origin. With no external torque it is exactly conserved. It takes no arguments.

`scene create` opens the graphical scene window. It starts a small HTTP and WebSocket server — hand-rolled on `std::net`, with no web framework — and prints the address to open in a browser. The window shows the bodies as wireframes, with a readout of energy, momentum and angular momentum that updates live.

The window evolves its **own copy** of the system. Stepping in the notebook does not move the window, and playing the window does not move the notebook. That isolation is deliberate.

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- `energy` was printed. Compare the value before the run with the value after it. For a closed system with no dissipation they should agree to near machine precision, and the size of the disagreement is the honest measure of the integration — not a number to be talked around.
- `momentum` was printed. With no external force the total linear momentum is exactly conserved, collisions included, because every impulse is applied equal and opposite.
- `angmom` was printed. With no external torque the total angular momentum about the origin is exactly conserved. Note that `L` is conserved, not `omega`: for a body whose three moments of inertia differ, the spin axis moves even though the angular momentum does not.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

inverse_mass = 0: a pinned anchor ignores gravity while a test body falls — dynamic notebook

Userguide Example S5: a mass-5 point at [0, 10, 0] made static by set inverse_mass = 0,
under uniform_gravity [0, -9.81, 0] with G = 0 — "three seconds of gravity, zero motion".
The coupled setters back-compute mass = 0, so the force m*g and the conversion p*m^-1
both vanish: the body is pinned at [0, 10, 0] forever.
DOCUMENTED ADAPTATION: S5 holds only the anchor; here one free point (mass 1 at [1, 10, 0])
stands beside it so the window shows the contrast — anchor pinned, neighbor falling
y(t) = 10 - 4.905 t^2: past y = 0 at t ~ 1.428 s, y = -34.145 at S5's t = 3 s.
Watch the hud: E stays 98.1 (kinetic and uniform-field potential trade exactly) while
P_y = -9.81 t and L_z = -9.81 t grow — gravity is external, so only E is conserved.
S5's caveat: mass 0 also stops SOURCING pairwise gravity (forces scale with G*mi*mj) —
use static bodies as anchors and test charges, not fixed suns (moot here: G = 0, as in S5).

Launch:   posim_notebook static_anchor
or:   cargo run -p posim --release -- --notebook dynamic_notebooks/static_anchor.posim
Press Start in the scene window (or type SCENE START here) to run
and display the simulation.
